He was received at the airport by Adylbek Kasymaliev, chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan, and welcomed with a traditional Kyrgyz dance performance.
The Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed Modi's arrival to participate in the SCO summit.
Before leaving India, Modi said he intends to advance India's vision for the region, focusing on security, connectivity and opportunity.
He emphasised the need for a region free from terrorism, separatism and extremism, which threaten peace and stability.
Russian President Putin is expected to hold separate talks with Iranian President Pezeshkian and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Modi, Xi and Putin last met at the SCO summit in Tianjin, China, in September 2025.
The leaders were seen sharing a warm interaction, with Modi and Putin travelling together in Putin's car.
This meeting drew attention as India-China ties were beginning to improve after years of tensions along the Line of Actual Control.

stories.headline: Glacier-rock collapse poses flood threat beyond GLOFs
stories.title: Glacier-rock collapse poses flood threat beyond GLOFs
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 30: The deadly August 26 flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border have drawn attention to a high-altitude hazard that can unleash destructive floods without a glacial lake - the sudden failure of glacier ice, rock and debris on an unstable slope. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said satellite analysis showed a high-magnitude glacier-rock collapse, or ice-rock avalanche, entering Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, before turning into a debris flood. The event was initially linked to a possible Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF). Subsequent satellite analysis and expert assessments pointed to an ice-rock avalanche associated with glacier and bedrock failure. Experts Seek Geological Mapping of Unstable Slopes Riyaz Ahmad Mir, a scientist at the National Institute of Hydrology's Western Himalayan Regional Centre (WHRC) in Jammu, said the source area had warm permafrost and fractured bedrock. "The failure entrained large volumes of glacier ice, snow and loose debris. It rapidly moved downstream and transformed into a highly destructive debris flood," Mir said. "Recent and prolonged warming, snow and glacier-ice melt, and increased water infiltration into bedrock fractures could have further weakened the slope. However, the direct contribution of climate change remains uncertain," he said. "These features now require identification and vulnerability assessment." Mir said Himachal Pradesh, the Chenab Valley in Jammu - Kishtwar, Doda and Ramban - and Ladakh should be priorities for detailed geological assessment followed by Kashmir. Prof Ghulam Jeelani, Dean of the School of Earth and Environmental Sciences at the University of Kashmir, said parts of Ladakh, including Zanskar, Shyok, and Nubra share similar high-altitude terrain. Jeelani explained glacier-rock collapses and GLOFs are separate processes. "Landslide or glacier collapse cannot create flash floods unless some surface water body, mountain river or water channel is there," he said. "The collapse itself does not require a glacial lake." He said an ice-rock avalanche can enter a river channel, pick up water, sediment and boulders and develop into a destructive debris flood. It can also strike a glacial lake, damage its natural dam and trigger a GLOF. "Thawing permafrost can weaken high-altitude slopes. Earthquakes, to which the Himalayan region is already at risk can trigger rockfalls, landslides and avalanches or damage natural dams," Jeelani said. Western Himalaya Warming A June 9 study published in the Journal of Earth System Science by researchers from BIT Mesra, IITM Pune and Ashoka University identified the Western Himalaya - J&K, Ladakh, and Himachal Pradesh - as the most climate-sensitive of the three Himalayan sectors examined. The study, Vulnerability of the Himalayan region under climate change, found the Western Himalaya has warmed by about 1 degree Celsius since the early 20th century. Under a high-emissions pathway, winter temperatures during 2081-2100 could rise by 7.18 degrees Celsius above early-20th-century levels. The study also warned that GLOF risk could shift westward as glaciers retreat and new glacial lakes form. A separate Department of Geoinformatics, University of Kashmir, study published in the Journal of Glaciology examined 155 glacial lakes in Kashmir using satellite data from 1992 to 2024. It identified Bramsar, Chirsar, Nundkol, Gangbal, and Bhagsar as having very high GLOF susceptibility. A preliminary assessment placed 2704 buildings and about 15 major bridges within potential impact zones. Roads and a hydropower project were also identified as exposed. The findings do not mean the lakes are on the verge of an outburst. They indicate higher susceptibility under specific triggering conditions. The study, however, does not cover unstable glacier-rock slopes that can fail independently of a glacial lake. Need for real-time alerts Mir said risk assessments must go beyond glacial-lake inventories. “The vulnerability assessment has to consider the entire system -the glacier, rock slope, permafrost, water, river channel and the downstream area,” he said. Experts called for detailed geological mapping of high-altitude slopes, fractured bedrock and permafrost zones. They also sought assessment of glacier stability, potential ice-rock avalanche paths and downstream debris-flood corridors. “Vulnerable sites should be monitored through satellite imagery and ground-based systems,” Mir said. “Real-time monitoring and early-warning systems are important in areas where sudden slope failures can threaten downstream settlements and infrastructure,” he said. For Jammu and Kashmir, Mir said Kishtwar is the main hotspot in the Chenab valley and faces high risk from both glacier-related hazards and GLOFs. Doda and Ramban also require assessment. Ladakh has the highest exposure to glacier-rock collapses and GLOFs, while Kashmir has lower GLOF exposure but remains vulnerable to glacier-rock collapses.

stories.headline: Powerful flash flood ravages Grand Canyon; 20 missing, 60 evacuated
stories.title: Video: Powerful flash flood ravages Grand Canyon; 20 missing, 60 evacuated
stories.summary: A fierce flash flood surged through Arizona's Grand Canyon on August 29, transforming Bright Angel Canyon and the Colorado River into raging torrents of debris-laden water. Reports confirm that at least twenty people are missing following this alarming occurrence. Over sixty individuals were evacuated from Phantom Ranch and Bright Angel Campground, leading to the closure of affected park areas, with officials requesting assistance from the public.

stories.headline: Nepal issues fresh flood warnings as Himalayan glacial disaster death toll touches 800 | VIDEO
stories.title: Nepal issues fresh flood warnings as Himalayan glacial disaster death toll touches 800 | VIDEO
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Rising river levels in Nepal trigger fresh flood warnings following a catastrophic glacial collapse that left hundreds dead.
Dhading (Nepal): Authorities in Nepal urged residents in flood-impacted districts to stay on high alert Sunday following a rise in water levels along the Bhotekoshi River.

Emergency notices were dispatched to mobile phones early in the day as rescue operations continued to clear access routes to areas devastated by Wednesday's catastrophic floods, which left at least 800 dead and thousands missing across Nepal and Tibet.

The renewed warnings were issued after Chinese officials alerted their Nepalese counterparts to increased water flow upstream, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Chinese state media, citing the country’s water resources ministry, reported that a newly formed high-altitude lake had largely drained.

However, officials warned that a separate crater containing an estimated 1.4 million cubic meters (370 million gallons) of water located 5.6 kilometers (3.5 miles) upstream continues to present potential risks.
Nepal’s disaster management agency reported Sunday that the domestic death toll had reached 788, with 2,502 people remaining missing.
Chinese authorities recorded 16 deaths and 546 missing on their side of the border.
Missing person reports include hundreds of foreign nationals, with Chinese media noting 261 foreigners missing in Tibet, including over 100 Nepalis.
In Dhading, one of the hardest-hit regions, survivors returned to damaged homes to assess losses and clear thick mud.

Critical infrastructure suffered extensive damage; a primary power plant supplying electricity to over 20,000 residents across four districts was knocked offline, leaving intact homes and businesses without power.
Destruction of major concrete and suspension bridges has isolated several local communities.

stories.headline: Iran President Pezeshkian to meet PM Modi during SCO Summit in Kyrgyzstan: Iranian media
stories.title: Iran President Pezeshkian to meet PM Modi during SCO Summit in Kyrgyzstan: Iranian media
stories.summary: Tehran , August 31: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is set to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his two-day visit to Kyrgyzstan for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit and SCO Plus meeting, Iran's state-run IRNA News Agency reported on Monday. According to IRNA, Pezeshkian left Tehran for Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, to participate in and address the SCO summit and the SCO Plus meeting. During his visit, the Iranian President will hold bilateral meetings with several participating leaders, including PM Modi, Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and the Presidents of Kyrgyzstan, Russia and Tajikistan. Pezeshkian will also attend the official opening ceremony of the 6th World Nomad Games at the invitation of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, IRNA reported. Prior to his departure, Pezeshkian said that Iran does not seek war, but will respond with strength and determination to any aggression. He considered instability in the region to be detrimental to all countries and emphasized the need for convergence to advance economic and security goals. "This meeting is very important and most of the leaders of the region will be present in it. In a situation where some international institutions are seeking to create a unified space in the world, this meeting is considered a symbol of the existence of diverse and independent voices in the global arena," he said. Emphasizing the ancient and civilized history of the countries of the region, the President stated: "We live in a region whose destiny, history, and civilization go back thousands of years, and we have always been in communication, coexistence, and growth with each other. Therefore, peace, security, economy, and civilization have arisen from this land, and it is natural that we should strive to expand this trend in today's world." Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Bishkek on Sunday, where he will participate in the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, marking the next leg of his two-country visit after concluding his state visit to Uzbekistan. The Prime Minister was received at the airport by Adylbek Kasymaliev, Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers of the Kyrgyz Republic. PM Modi is visiting Bishkek at the invitation of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov. The 26th SCO Summit will bring together leaders of member states to deliberate on regional and international issues and ways to further strengthen cooperation within the grouping. The Prime Minister is also scheduled to hold several bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the summit.

stories.headline: US strikes Iranian rocket launchers on Strait of Hormuz in first military action in weeks
stories.title: US strikes Iranian rocket launchers on Strait of Hormuz in first military action in weeks
stories.summary: Washington, Aug 31: US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in their first military action in a month on Sunday, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months. Iran swiftly vowed to retaliate for what it called a deadly attack. Forces with the Revolutionary Guard Corps were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for the US Central Command. The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes. Semiofficial news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The Guard in a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots.” A return to open conflict would be dangerous for the region, where Iran has targeted US military bases and infrastructure in Gulf countries since the war began on February 28. The last time the US military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, when it announced a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets including coastal surveillance and defence sites. On August 1, President Donald Trump said he would order the military to hold off on new strikes at the urging of Gulf allies Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. The US had turned to economic pressure The attack comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure — rather than military action — to try to end its war with Iran. The shifting strategy centres on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran. Sunday's attack was a “fatal mistake by the Trump regime during the economic war” and the enemy will pay the consequences militarily and economically, a Guard spokesperson, Gen. Hossein Mohebi, said in a statement carried by Iranian media. The US turn to using sanctions came as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine US military readiness in other parts of the globe. As the conflict grinds on, Trump's talk of finding a quick end to the war also appears to be fading. He stressed last week that he's “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic's leadership is on the ropes. Appointments to Iran's senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signalled Tehran's defiance after weathering decades of sanctions as well as a lack of tolerance for dissent at home. Trump has consistently emphasised that the US and Israel campaign has been devastating for Iran's navy and air force. Iranian officials have said the country has suffered USD 270 billion in direct and indirect damage. Israeli military strikes in the first weeks of the war wiped out much of the theocratic government's leadership structure. Iran leans on the strait for leverage But Iran has found leverage through its strikes against vessels on the Strait of Hormuz, where relatively few ships carrying oil and liquefied natural gas are risking passage. Iran still has enough drones and missiles to fire at vessels transiting the waterway through which 20 per cent of the world's oil normally flows. Tehran continues to assert that even after it works out a management plan for the strait with Oman, its neighbor on the other side of the waterway, the US can't use it until it fulfils its obligations under the memorandum of understanding the countries signed in mid-June. Trump has repeatedly declared that the “Strait of Hormuz is open,” saying 24 vessels passed through last week. But that's a fraction of the roughly 130 vessels that transited daily before the war began. Earlier on Sunday, a multinational coalition overseen by the US Navy said commercial traffic through the strait remained at “reduced levels.” And a monitoring agency run by the British military said an unknown projectile struck a tanker ship on Saturday north of Khasab, Oman, in the strait. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said no casualties or environmental impact had been reported, and cited unspecified military authorities. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. The US military said that as of Sunday, it had redirected 83 commercial vessels and disabled three under its blockade of Iranian ports. (AP)

stories.headline: J&K businesses seek SBI-style OTS to break legacy debt cycle
stories.title: J&K businesses seek SBI-style OTS to break legacy debt cycle
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 30: Businesses and businessmen in Jammu and Kashmir are seeking a comprehensive one-time settlement (OTS) scheme on the lines of the State Bank of India’s 2020 framework, arguing that more than three decades of disruption have left enterprises struggling with legacy debt despite repeated restructuring and relief measures. Business chambers across Kashmir have called for authorities to facilitate a broader settlement mechanism with J&K Bank, saying borrowers have operated under extraordinary conditions since 1989 and should be provided an opportunity for financial closure. The business community has cited recurring curfews, shutdowns, violence, communication restrictions, the 2014 floods, the 2016 unrest, the constitutional changes of 2019 and the COVID-19 pandemic as major disruptions to economic activity. They contend that while businesses were unable to operate normally for prolonged periods, interest on outstanding loans continued to accumulate, leaving many businessmen with liabilities far beyond their original repayment capacity. The demand, however, is not for a blanket loan waiver. Business chambers are seeking a transparent, non-discretionary and formula-based settlement mechanism under which eligible borrowers would pay a predetermined amount, have their accounts closed after settlement and exit prolonged litigation and recovery proceedings. The proposal comes against the backdrop of J&K Bank’s central role in financing the regional economy. The bank has historically supported tourism, horticulture, trade, transport, manufacturing, handicrafts and small businesses, particularly in areas where other financial institutions maintained a relatively limited presence. Business organisations argue that this created a close relationship between the bank and the regional economy, with J&K Bank’s deposit base and lending activity substantially linked to J&K. Some businessmen have also alleged that borrowers in J&K were charged higher interest rates than comparable businesses elsewhere and were required to provide substantial collateral and personal guarantees. The exact differential in lending rates would require verification from bank records, but business organisations say the issue warrants greater transparency. The 2014 floods brought the scale of business distress into sharp focus. Several enterprises lost shops, machinery, inventories and other assets, while their loan liabilities continued to remain outstanding. Subsequent relief measures largely included moratoriums, restructuring, funded-interest arrangements and interest assistance rather than outright settlement. Similar restructuring measures followed the 2016 unrest and disruptions after August 2019. Businessmen argue that restructuring cannot be treated as equivalent to settlement. When unpaid interest is converted into a funded-interest term loan, they say, the liability is postponed rather than extinguished. For enterprises repeatedly affected by circumstances beyond their control, restructuring can therefore result in a prolonged cycle of accumulated debt. The business community has pointed to SBI’s history of OTS schemes as a possible model. SBI introduced structured settlement schemes in 2010, 2012, 2014, 2016-17, 2017, 2019, and 2020. Its OTS-2020, launched on October 12, 2020, covered eligible non-performing and recovery accounts with dues above Rs 20 lakh and up to Rs 50 crore as of March 31, 2020. The scheme prescribed objective eligibility criteria, a predetermined settlement formula, upfront payment requirements and incentives for early settlement. It also provided for resolution of eligible litigated accounts through consent orders. The SBI framework was formulated within the regulatory framework governing stressed-asset resolution. The Reserve Bank of India’s Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets, issued on June 7, 2019, recognised compromise settlements as a possible mechanism for resolution, subject to board-approved policies of banks. The RBI subsequently issued its Framework for Compromise Settlements and Technical Write-offs on June 8, 2023, aimed at providing further impetus to the resolution of stressed assets and harmonising practices across regulated entities. J&K Bank has also introduced OTS initiatives, including the Karz Mukti scheme in 2022 and subsequent schemes with expanded categories and limits. Business representatives acknowledge these measures but argue that they have not provided a sufficiently broad mechanism for resolving older legacy accounts. The business chambers are therefore seeking a wider settlement window based on objective eligibility, a defined formula, specified upfront payment, incentives for early settlement, inclusion of appropriate litigated accounts and fixed timelines for disposal. They have also called for a temporary pause on coercive recovery measures against borrowers who are prima facie eligible and have formally applied for settlement. Such a pause, they argue, need not provide permanent immunity, with lawful recovery able to resume if borrowers fail to comply with settlement conditions. The ownership structure of the two banks has also figured in the debate. The Government of India holds around 55 percent of SBI, while the J&K government holds around 59 percent of J&K Bank’s equity. Business representatives argue that the government, as a major shareholder in J&K Bank and an important stakeholder in the region’s economic revival, can facilitate a broader discussion on the issue, although it cannot direct the bank to settle individual loan accounts. The business community has called for consultations involving J&K Bank, business chambers, representatives of tourism, horticulture, transport and other affected sectors, economists and stressed borrowers. They have also sought an assessment of the region’s legacy business debt. The broader argument is that J&K businesses are not seeking exemption from financial discipline but a mechanism to achieve finality. Businessmen say repeated restructuring has provided temporary relief in several cases without resolving the underlying debt burden. They argue that an SBI-style OTS could provide a structured route to close old accounts, reduce prolonged litigation and recovery proceedings, revive potentially viable enterprises and restore their access to institutional credit. For the business community, the demand is therefore being framed not simply as a concession but as a financial-resolution mechanism aimed at giving enterprises that survived decades of disruption an opportunity to start again without the weight of accumulated legacy debt.

stories.headline: Megha Engg's PVK Reddy taps $700 mn credit
stories.title: Megha Engg's PVK Reddy taps $700 mn credit
stories.summary: A key shareholder of India’s Megha Engineering & Infrastructures Ltd. is seeking to raise about $700 million from global private credit investors to buy out his uncle’s stake in the company, according to people familiar with the matter, in what would be one of the nation’s biggest deals this year.A consortium of lenders including Davidson Kempner Capital Management, Elham Credit Partners and Varde Partners has begun preliminary work on the structure of the financing, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. Terms haven’t been finalized and discussions could still change, they said.Billionaire PV Krishna Reddy, the managing director of Megha Engineering who now owns 57% of the company is raising the money to help finance his acquisition of the remaining 43% stake held by his uncle Pamireddy Pitchi Reddy, the executive chairman, according to one of the people.Representatives for Megha Engineering, Elham Credit Partners and Varde Partners didn’t respond to Bloomberg’s requests for comment. Davidson Kempner declined to comment.If completed, it would be among India’s largest private credit deals this year, and just under half of the equivalent $1.6 billion raised by conglomerate Shapoorji Pallonji Group last month. The planned deal highlights the growing role of private credit in financing large shareholder and corporate transactions in India, where traditional lenders could be constrained in offering flexibility on funding certain types of acquisitions.Also read | Iran crisis puts Xi-Putin’s anti-US bloc to the testInvestments in the country’s private credit market reached $3.5 billion in the first half of 2026, less than half of the $9 billion in deals a year earlier which included the record $3.1 billion raised by Shapoorji Pallonji Group for refinancing, a report from consulting firm EY shows.India’s private credit sector has doubled in size over the past five years to about $25 billion in assets under management at the end of 2025, according to Moody’s Ratings. Although that pales in comparison with the US market, which manages more than $1 trillion in assets.Founded in 1989 as a small fabrication unit in Hyderabad, Megha Engineering has projects in more than 20 countries spanning tunnels, ports, highways, water systems and power assets, according to its website.Also read | Nepal disaster puts focus on what China did not shareThe company has been seeking to sell some of its road assets. KKR & Co.-backed Vertis Infrastructure Trust has emerged as the frontrunner to acquire eight roads from Megha, Bloomberg reported in July.Megha was the top donor to Bharatiya Janata Party over the past five years, according to a 2024 election commission data, purchasing about Rs 670 crore ($70 million) of electoral bonds.

stories.headline: Trouble in the Himalayas!
stories.title: Trouble in the Himalayas!
stories.summary: It was like doomsday in neighboring country Nepal on August 26 when catastrophic flash floods and mudslides were triggered by a massive glacier and rock collapse near Langtang Lirung in the Himalayan region. Flash floods led to the death of at least 734 with nearly 2,500 people still missing with massive destruction of houses, bridges and infrastructure. The US Geological Survey states that the disaster was caused by a “glacial collapse”— when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates. It is stated that the impact of the collapsed glacier hitting downstream was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2. The international Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), an intergovernmental scientific institution, revealed that there could have been an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude area. This is caused when a“large volume of ice and rock debris” entered the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, which in turn generated a sudden surge in the river carrying water, sediment and large boulders downstream. The centre revealed that water levels in rivers downstream rose by between seven and nine metres within a span of 30 minutes, and several water monitoring stations were washed away or damaged. What is concerning is that the Hindu Kush Himalayan glaciers have been retreating double the rate since 2000 exacerbating flash floods. This year Jammu and Kashmir witnessed increase in flash floods causing loss of over 30 lives and destruction of infrastructure. On July 2, 12 cloudbursts were reported in 12 hours when the southwest monsoon arrived in J&K. On July 7 we witnessed massive flash floods in Thathri town of Jammu’s Doda district. The intensity of flash floods was such that gushing waters carried boulders, rocks and tons of soil burying several houses and vehicles. On July 10, flash floods hit Ari Sarhuti village of Mendhar in Poonch district after heavy rainfall in the area with water damaging human habitations and agriculture fields, On July 11 flash floods caused sudden rise in water level in Oowera area of Pahalgam, damaging several huts and hotels. On August 14 last year 65 people were killed, 120 injured and 30 are still missing after a cloudburst-triggered flash flood swept through Chisoti village in Paddar-Gulabgarh tehsil of Kishtwar district in Jammu region. The incident had occurred when devotees on way to pay obeisance at Machail Mata temple were struck by flash floods following cloudbursts in the upper reaches of Chisoti village. Studies identify the western Himalaya - covering Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh - as the most climate-sensitive of the three Himalayan sectors. The western Himalaya has warmed by about 1 degree Celsius since the early 20th century. The western Himalaya is projected to experience the sharpest snow loss, with implications for glacier retreat, meltwater flows and downstream water availability. The prolonged heat wave and dry spells in J&K are taking a heavy toll on glaciers. The drought-like situation in the last 5 years has expedited the retreating of most of the glaciers in the Kashmir Himalaya. Kolahoi, the largest glacier of Kashmir’s Jhelum Basin, has been melting rapidly due to a spurt in temperature triggered by global warming and extreme pollution. Thajiwas, Hoksar, Nehnar, Shishram, and glaciers around Harmukh are melting fast. Fast retreating of glaciers because of global warming and pollution has created glacial lakes, which can be disastrous, in various mountain ranges of J&K besides Ladakh. There is a massive risk of Glacial Lake Outburst Floods in Kashmir. Melting glaciers erode land and fill up the space, creating glacial lakes. Five glacial lakes in the Kashmir Himalaya pose a very high risk of sudden, catastrophic GLOFs as per a ground-breaking research led by researchers from the University of Kashmir. The study warns that “such events could wipe out communities and critical infrastructure downstream of glacial lakes.” The study, conducted by satellite remote sensing and a novel framework, assessed lakes based on 10 risk factors, including dam material, slope stability, seismic activity, permafrost thaw, and upstream cascades. It reveals that lakes like Bramsar and Chirsar are “ticking time bombs.” The hydrologically-linked Nundkol and Gangabal lakes from the Ganderbal district alone threaten more than 1000 buildings, four bridges, and a hydropower plant. Bramsar and Chirsar lakes together endanger at least more than 400 buildings and five bridges in the south Kashmir districts of Shopian and Kulgam, while Bhagsar Lake puts more than 1100 structures, and six bridges, at risk in Shopian district. GLOF risk is currently concentrated in the central Himalaya, but it is projected to shift and triple towards the western Himalaya by the end of the century, putting Kashmir directly in the crosshairs of this escalating climate threat. Kashmir has no recorded history of major GLOFs, but the physical conditions are now aligning dangerously. In seismically active Zone V terrain with widespread permafrost, a single breach could trigger multi-hazard cascades downstream. Chairing a high-level review meeting in the aftermath of heavy rains, landslides, and floods in J&K, Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Amit Shah, on September 1 last year, had emphasised the urgent need to strengthen GLOF and cloudburst early warning systems. He had stressed that a critical analysis of existing Early Warning Apps (EWAs), their accuracy, and grassroots reach was vital to moving toward a “zero-casualty” approach. The J&K Government has also outlined a roadmap that included continuous remote-sensing and field monitoring, installation of early-warning systems, bathymetric surveys planned for 2026, development of ecozonation plans, and integration of GLOF scenarios into district disaster plans. The work on mountain-specific early-warning prototypes that combine satellite data, field observations and real-time sensors is already underway at University of Kashmir. We need to understand that we cannot prevent GLOF or flash floods but can minimise damage by early developing warning mechanisms. Also hydropower and other river engineering structures downstream should be designed to withstand the disastrous surges of the water and debris associated with the bursting of the glacier lakes, particularly in the Chenab Valley, where several hydropower projects are in operation. There is also a need to strengthen our disaster management mechanism. We need to develop a disaster resilient society in view of the increase in natural disasters induced by climate change. We need to learn to live with the changing weather patterns in the Himalayas of which are an integral part! Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: Violence plummeted, security improved in J&K: NITI Aayog
stories.title: Violence plummeted, security improved in J&K: NITI Aayog
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 30: Jammu and Kashmir has witnessed a sharp decline in several key indicators of terrorism and violence, with stone-pelting incidents dropping by 98.6 percent and youth recruitment into terrorism has also declined by 99 percent between 2018 and 2025. The NITI Aayog figures produced on significant improvement in Law and Order compares compares key security indicators between 2018 and 2025 and points to a substantial reduction in violence-related incidents across J&K. As per the figures, stone-pelting incidents have declined from 1767 reported in 2018 to only 25 in 2025 which shows a 98.6 percent reduction in such incidents. Similarly, youth recruitment in terrorism has also witnessed a sharp decline from 199 cases reported in 2018 to only two in 2025 which is around 99 percent reduction. Also, the number of terrorist-initiated incidents have also declined sharply from 228 in 2018 to 12 in 2025 which is almost a 95 percent decline in such incidents. The NITI Aayog data further shows that counter-terror operations and encounters have also come down from 189 in 2018 to 33 in 2025 which is an 82.5 percent decline. As per the figures, the number of terrorists killed has declined from 257 to 34 from 2018 to 2025 which is around 87 percent reduction in such incidents. The number of security forces personnel martyred in terrorist incidents and encounters has also dropped from 91 in 2018 to 16 in 2025 showing a decline of 82.4 percent in such violence related incidents. As per the NITI Aayog figures, civilian casualties have also witnessed a substantial decline as the number of civilians killed in terrorist incidents or encounters has declined from 55 in 2018 to 28 in 2025. The reduction is around 49.1 percent. However the number of terrorist associates or suspects arrested have shown an increase from 105 in 2018 to 143 in 2025. The action has witnessed an increase of 36.2 percent, showcasing intensified action against the support network associated with terrorism. As per the official figures, there has been a decline in ceasefire violations from 382 in 2018 to 193 in 2025 which is a reduction by 49.5 percent. Referring to Operation Sindoor, the NITI Aayog figures have pointed out administrative and relief response during the Operation Sindoor in May 2025, following LoC shelling between May 7 and 10 of 2025. As per the official figures, Poonch, Rajouri, Jammu, Baramulla, and Kupwara were identified as severely affected districts. In wake of this authorities took proactive administrative measures during the operation. "As part of the coordinated response to the LoC shelling, 3.26 lakh persons were evacuated while 397 relief centres were established and 15,293 persons were lodged in these centres," read the NITI Aayog figures. As per the figures, health services were activated and 394 ambulances were mobilised besides activating 2818 Civil Defence volunteers to assist the response. "The authorities also activated 9,701 bunkers besides taking measures to protect infrastructure, ensure supplies and prevent hoarding," the document reads. stories.headline: Assam govt to invest Rs 50,000 crore in developing infra over 5 yrs: Himanta
stories.title: Assam govt to invest Rs 50,000 crore in developing infra over 5 yrs: Himanta
stories.summary: Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said the state government will invest Rs 50,000 crore over five years under ‘Viksit Assam: Infra Vision’ to develop infrastructure across sectors, including healthcare, education, roads, power, housing, markets and flood protection
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: Guwahati: The Assam government will invest Rs 50,000 crore over the next five years to develop infrastructure across sectors, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said.

Addressing a press conference after a state cabinet meeting here on Sunday, Sarma said the investment would cover primary healthcare, schools, anganwadi centres, housing for tea garden workers, power, roads, women markets and hostels, besides flood embankments.
“The state cabinet has approved pumping in Rs 50,000 crore for ‘Viksit Assam: Infra Vision’.
Under this scheme, we will be developing various infrastructures across the state,” he said.

Sarma said the cabinet also approved allotment of 1,174 bighas of land in Kamrup Metropolitan and Nagaon districts to the Industries, Commerce and Public Enterprises Department for developing industrial estates and land banks.
The government will also allot 27 bighas in Rangajan Gaon in Dhemaji district to the Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Department for setting up a milk project, he said.

The CM said that to improve the ease of doing business, the cabinet approved the Assam Trade Articles (Licensing and Control) (Amendment) Order, 2026, abolishing the requirement of retail selling licences for petroleum products.

It also approved an amendment to the Industrial and Investment Policy of Assam, 2019, to include Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facilities as an eligible industrial activity for fiscal incentives under the Assam Vehicle Scrappage Policy, 2022.

The cabinet extended the one-time window for determining the market value of tea gardens or tea land for calculating stamp duty and registration fees on conveyance deeds, along with the one-time SOP valuation mechanism, he said.

The cabinet also approved a Rs 300-crore project by Fermbox Bio Pvt Ltd at Tezpur in Sonitpur district and an integrated 30 MW solar power and 25 MW Battery Energy Storage System project at Rakhyasini Jungle Block in Goalpara district.

An amount of Rs 155.98 crore was sanctioned for construction of a rail overbridge near Hawaipur station and a bypass road connecting Kheroni Chariali in West Karbi Anglong with NH-27 at Bamungaon, Sarma said.
The project is expected to ease congestion in Lanka town.
